A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same BASE/G-BASE study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–H support reliable comparison, including matching relocated content.

before.justification: v1 reports original membership-inference experiments on six graph datasets and CIFAR-10/100, including baseline comparisons, threshold calibration, robustness tests, and sampling analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports revised graph results, additional sampling diagnostics, and inference-time measurements.

M1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds Gibbs sampling as a fourth membership-mask sampling strategy for G-BASE, using sequential conditional membership updates. The practical BASE and G-BASE score formulas and existing sampling strategies remain, making this a limited procedural extension.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, Flickr, Amazon-Photo, Github, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 on the same graph-node and i.i.d. membership-inference tasks. The added diagnostics and changed model configurations do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes both MLP baseline variants, 0-hop and 0+2-hop, from the K=128 comparisons across all six graph datasets. They remain in the K=8 comparisons. LiRA and RMIA remain the principal statistical baselines.

E3.justification: Section 6 changes large-K G-BASE evaluations from 32 sampled graphs, or 16 for Flickr/Github, to 8. Offline BASE/RMIA hyperparameter selection changes from one simulated target to cross-validation over shadow models. Table 9 revises model configurations and online/offline comparisons; new protocols evaluate oracle masks, varying sample counts, and inference time. These are substantial reported evaluation changes.

E4.justification: The earlier three-sampler comparison is substantially expanded and revised in v2 Appendix H.2/Table 9, adding Gibbs sampling, ground-truth membership-mask diagnostics, and offline comparisons. New Table 10 tests sensitivity to 4–32 graph samples, and Table 11 examines computational cost. Threshold-calibration and mismatched-adversary analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 drop v1's explicit 'population' qualification for standard deviation, leaving its normalization unspecified. Both versions retain mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting over ten target models. This is a limited loss of statistical reporting specificity, not evidence of a changed estimator or increased run count.

E6.justification: Graph benchmark and robustness results change extensively in Tables 1, 2, and 8; for example, reported Cora/GCN K=8 BASE AUC changes from 81.48% to 82.45%. Gibbs, oracle-mask, sample-count, and timing results are added, while some earlier entries disappear. CIFAR results remain unchanged, moving from Table 10 to Table 12. Revised settings prevent treating all numerical differences as comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 now retains a prior likelihood-ratio term Lambda and explicitly integrates over models conditioned on the target being absent. Appendix B.1 replaces the earlier approximate cancellation with a revised derivation; setting Lambda=1 becomes an explicit practical approximation in Section 4.3. Corollary 1 additionally states the membership-independence assumption on the prior. These substantially revise the central theoretical foundation.

C1.justification: The main contributions remain, but their scope is qualified. The abstract describes both attacks as tractable rather than computationally efficient approximations; the introduction says they tend to match or outperform alternatives, especially on larger datasets. It also removes the explicit contribution claim that BASE outperforms RMIA offline.

C2.justification: New computational discussion explains G-BASE's inability to batch target-node inference and its additional N×M cost, substantially qualifying practicality. Section 6 and Appendix F revise the online/offline interpretation: the theoretical reference distribution excludes the target, although practical approximations may benefit from in-models. Appendix H.2 also develops the explanation of noisy shadow-model signals limiting gains from better sampling.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies target-training and audit-node fractions, balanced membership sampling, and the 20% audit subset exception for large-K Flickr/Github experiments. It documents one Gibbs sweep and a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance-rate target of 0.2–0.4. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit 1000-step burn-in, 500-step spacing, and 50% MLP edge-dropout specification. These omissions do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds Watson et al.'s work on difficulty calibration, credits prior work for simulated-target threshold selection in Appendix C, and relates mean-confidence calibration to that literature in Appendix E.3. The broader related-work survey and research positioning remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Explanations of approximations, experiments, and online/offline attacks receive localized rewrites. Appendix H is reorganized, moving ROC discussion from H.1 to H.5, and the preprint header becomes a NeurIPS 2025 header. The main section sequence and substantial portions of the prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially restructures Tables 1 and 9, adds sample-count and runtime Tables 10–11, redraws ROC plots and legends, and adds the Github ROC Figure 7. Appendix ROC displays are relocated, and Figure 6 changes from Flickr/GraphSAGE to Flickr/GAT. The existing CIFAR table is retained as Table 12. Together these substantially revise the empirical displays.

improvement.justification: v1 presents its central theorem as exact despite an approximate prior cancellation in its proof. v2 retains that prior ratio and explicitly separates practical approximations, materially improving mathematical transparency. The oracle-mask, sample-count, and timing studies also address important gaps in validating approximation quality and computational claims, including G-BASE's substantial overhead. These gains outweigh the narrower losses of sampling details and high-K MLP comparisons.
